Salakas Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Utena County, Lithuania

Not demolished. Salakas grew into a trading town in the 19th century, with over 30 Jewish-owned stores and pubs and an economy built on agricultural trade, timber, fishing, and pottery production; the Jewish population reached 1,582 (66 percent) by 1897. After WWI, new borders cut Salakas off from Vilnius, driving many Jews to emigrate to South Africa, Cuba, and Israel; the Zionist Socialist party was especially active locally. Among the rabbis who served Salakas was Rabbi Shmuel Mohliver (1824–1898), a leading figure of religious Zionism — the kibbutz Gan-Shemuel in Israel is named after him. Another notable native, Dr. Aryeh Behm (1877–1941), emigrated to Israel, where he established the first Pasteur Institute in Jerusalem and helped found the Medical Council there. During the Holocaust, Salakas's Jews were murdered in the nearby Sungardai forest; a memorial at the site commemorates 114 victims killed there in August 1941. This cemetery, registered in Lithuania's Cultural Property Register in 1999, holds about 570 surviving tombstones and the remains of a pre-war masonry wall; a memorial stone was erected in 1991.
